newsitem.title: USA: Scorecard needed to track US bond primary dealers.
newsitem.headline: Scorecard needed to track US bond primary dealers.

text.p: Over the past two weeks, the Federal Reserve has had to issue two changes to its list of primary dealers in U.S. Treasury securities, and experts said they expect more changes over the next few months.

The Fed now lists 39 firms as primary dealers, down from a peak of 46 in the late 1980s. But analysts said they do not expect recent changes in primary dealer ranks to have a major imapct on the market unless one of the giants -- which include Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc, Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, Salomon Brothers and Lehman Bros -- drops out.

The largest 10 primary dealers control the bulk of activity, and the possibility that one may drop out no longer sounds as far-fetched as it once did, analyts said. Sources within the industry noted that the largest dealers were prime candidates for takeovers or mergers, given that many of their smaller competitors were merging, thereby becoming larger and stronger.

"You need to be bigger and in a position to take on risk to (be profitable)," said Ted Stevens, managing director and financial services analyst at PNC Asset Management. "Spreads are compressing, so it is harder to make it on a buy it, mark it up, and resell it business."
Plus, he said, an increasing leveraged nature of the fixed income markets has added volatility and risk.

Consequently, over the past few years so many dealers have merged that it requies a scorecard. Among them were Kidder Peabody and PaineWebber Group Inc, and Swiss Bank Corp and S.G. Warburg (which sold its dealership to CIBC Wood Gundy). As for dealers who are also banks, Manufacturers Hanover and Chemical merged, and later Chemical and Chase Manhattan Corp.
Most recently, in February, Dean Witter Discover & Co announced a merger with Morgan Stanley, and on Thursday, Dillon Read and Swiss Bank's SBC Warburg said they would combine forces.

Various mergers over the years reduced the number of primary dealers, with the recent Dean Witter-Morgan Stanley and Dillon Read-SBC Warburg deals thinning the ranks further. Plus, NationsBank said last week it plans to sell its primary dealership. And analyts said Japan's Nippon Credit Bank may sell its Eastbridge Capital unit as part of a retreat from the international arena it announced April 1.
Peter Bakstansky, senior vice president at the New York Fed said the number of primary dealers has no bearing on the Fed's daily open market operations.
"We can do business with 38, 37; we have done business with as many as 46 and as little as 20," he said. "The market is deep enough and there is enough depth and strength for us to get our job done."

Bakstansky said there is really nothing overly special about being a primary dealer; it is just an agreement to be a counterparty to the New York Fed in open market operations. He noted that non-dealers still may bid at Treasury auctions.
Primary dealers, though, are required to "meaningfully" participate at auctions, and have a minimal capital requirement -- $50 million for non-banks and $100 million for banks.

"There is no free ride in being a dealer," said Morton Swinsky, president and chief executive officer at Fuji Securities. "You just have access to the Fed for open market operations. You don't get to go to the White House and take your picture with President Clinton like the Yankees did last year."

Actually, officials at some dealers said there is little benefit in being a primary dealer given the many regulations the Fed imposes. Still, U.S. primary dealership is said to benefit foreign-owned firms most since they get access to the U.S. market.

"European firms are trying to get a foothold in the large capital market that exists in the U.S.," said Mark Bachmann, managing director of the financial institutions group at Standard & Poor's. "But it is hard to do. The Japanese talked about getting into the U.S. business in a big way but realized it was a hard thing to do."
Still, French-owned Banque Paribas PBAZ.S and German-based Dresdner Bank AG unit Dresdner Kleinwort Benson became primary dealers in the past few weeks.

"If you want to put the word 'global' before 'securities firm,' you have to cross through the dollar," Stevens said. "This is the land of opportunity for securities firms, just like it is for everyone who wants to emigrate here."
